sections.h2: Who inherits a Missouri house when there is no will?
sections.html:
The answer depends on whether the owner left a spouse and whether any children came from outside that marriage. RSMo 474.010 sets the order of descent for property a person leaves without a will, and a house is distributed under the same order as everything else in the estate.

A surviving spouse takes the whole intestate estate when the decedent had no surviving children or other issue. If there are children and every one of them is also a child of the surviving spouse, the spouse receives the first $20,000 plus half of what remains. If at least one child is not the spouse's, the spouse receives one half.

Whatever the spouse does not take, or the whole estate when there is no spouse, moves down a list:

  • the decedent's children, or their descendants, in equal parts;
  • if there are none, the parents, brothers and sisters or their descendants;
  • then grandparents, uncles and aunts or their descendants;
  • then great-grandparents and onward to the nearest lineal ancestors and their descendants, with collateral relatives limited to the ninth degree of kinship.

If nobody qualifies, the statute sends the property to the kindred of a predeceased spouse, and failing that, the property escheats. Co-heirs who inherit a house this way own it together, which is why a sale usually needs every one of them to sign.

sections.h2: When can a Missouri estate skip full probate?
sections.html:
A small estate can pass by affidavit when everything left, after subtracting liens, debts and encumbrances, does not exceed $40,000. RSMo 473.097 lists the conditions: thirty days must have gone by since the death, with no application for letters pending or granted; a bond approved by the judge or clerk of the probate division must be filed, though the court may dispense with it; and the filing fee, plus newspaper publication cost where it applies, must be paid.

The person signing the affidavit is the personal representative named in a probated will or, otherwise, a distributee. The affidavit describes and values the property, names who holds it and who will receive it, and states that debts and any estate tax will be paid. The clerk attaches a certificate naming the people entitled to each item. For a house, the distributees prove their right to the real estate by recording the affidavit and certificate with the recorder of deeds in each county where the land lies.

If the property in the affidavit exceeds $15,000, the clerk publishes a notice to creditors once a week for two consecutive weeks. After the procedure is complete, the property cannot be taken in execution for the decedent's debts, though a secured creditor keeps its rights. The $40,000 ceiling is low next to most house values, so many estates that include a home will need letters from the court instead.

sections.h2: What deadlines apply to a will and to creditors?
sections.html:
A will has no effect until it is presented to the probate division and admitted. Under RSMo 473.050, presenting means delivering the will, or a verified statement about a lost one, along with a petition or a small estate affidavit asking for admission. If no notice of the granting of letters has been given, the will must be presented within one year of the date of death. Where that notice has been published, the window is six months after first publication. A will that misses the time limit is barred from probate in Missouri.

Letters of administration follow a related clock: with limited exceptions, the court will not issue them unless the application is made within one year of death. This is the number to keep in mind when an heir inherits a house years after a parent died and nothing was ever filed.

Creditors have their own limit. RSMo 473.444 makes most claims against a decedent unenforceable one year after death whether or not an estate was opened and whether or not the creditor knew. Costs of administration, exempt property, family and homestead allowances, claims of the United States and claims of any taxing authority are carved out, and a mortgage or other lien on the property can still be enforced. A lienholder on the house is therefore a separate question from an unsecured creditor.

sections.h2: Who can sign a deed to sell an inherited house in Missouri?
sections.html:
The person with authority to sign depends on how the estate is being handled. When the court has issued letters, the personal representative acts for the estate. When a small estate affidavit is used, the distributees named in the clerk's certificate record that paperwork and then hold the title for the sale. A buyer or title company will want to see whichever document applies before it will insure the sale.

One workaround is worth knowing. RSMo 461.025 allows a beneficiary deed, a deed that states it does not take effect until the owner dies. It transfers the interest to the named grantee at death if it was signed and filed with the recorder of deeds before the owner died. It needs no consideration and does not have to be delivered to the grantee, and it can name a trust as the grantee. A deed that is valid on other grounds is not defeated just because it was recorded after the owner's death.

The county circuit court's probate division handles letters, small estate affidavits and creditor notices. Ask that court's clerk for the local filing steps and fee schedule, since procedures are applied county by county.

sections.h2: What should heirs do before selling an inherited Missouri house?
sections.html:
Begin by finding out whether a will exists and whether it was presented to the probate division in time. Then work out the value of the whole estate after liens, because that figure decides whether the small estate route is open. The mortgage balance and any other lien on the home reduce the number for that test, while ownership held jointly with right of survivorship is outside the decedent's property for the affidavit.

  • Order certified death certificates and gather the deed, the mortgage statement and the latest tax bill.
  • Ask the probate clerk whether letters have been requested and whether the one-year application window remains open.
  • List every heir in line under RSMo 474.010 if no will exists, since each one may need to sign.
  • Record the affidavit and clerk's certificate with the county recorder of deeds before listing or closing, if the small estate route applies.
  • Check for open claims against the estate while the one-year creditor limit is running.

Because the paperwork differs by county, a call to the probate division clerk and to the recorder of deeds before you list saves weeks later.

faqs.q: What is the largest estate that can use the Missouri small estate affidavit?
faqs.a: The ceiling is $40,000 after subtracting liens, debts and encumbrances. RSMo 473.097 also requires thirty days to have passed since the death with no application for letters pending or granted, a bond unless the court waives it, and payment of the fee.

faqs.q: Does a surviving spouse inherit everything in Missouri?
faqs.a: Only when the decedent left no surviving children or other issue. If all the children are also the spouse's, the spouse takes the first $20,000 plus half of the rest, and if any child is from another relationship the spouse takes half, all under RSMo 474.010.

faqs.q: How long do I have to present a will to the court?
faqs.a: Within one year of the date of death when no notice of letters has been given, or six months after the first publication of notice of letters. RSMo 473.050 bars a will that misses its window, and letters of administration generally require an application within one year of death.

faqs.q: Do I have to record anything with the county to sell inherited land?
faqs.a: If the small estate affidavit is used, yes. Distributees establish their right to the real estate by recording a copy of the affidavit and the clerk's certificate with the recorder of deeds in each county where the property sits, as RSMo 473.097 provides.

faqs.q: Can an owner avoid probate for a house before dying?
faqs.a: A beneficiary deed under RSMo 461.025 can do that. It must say it is not to take effect until the owner's death and be filed with the recorder of deeds in the county where the real property is located before the owner dies.
